source_read: PDF of the PubMed Central author manuscript, AM pp. 1-19 (all pages; Figures 1-3 and Table 4 checked on rendered pages). References 51-95 (Appendix 1) and Supplemental Tables 1-3 are web-only supplements and were not read, so refs 51-95 cannot be identified.

claims.overstatement: The claim is more cautious than the review, which treats change after a positive strip as an effect (a positive strip 'likely results in a net increase' in safer behaviour, AM p. 7; widely documented, AM p. 8). One phrase is not Kutscher's: 'mostly intentions'. Kutscher files most documented changes under actual behaviour after a result (Table 4), although that column includes staff-recorded intentions (Vancouver, ref. 69) and the take-home survey's standard-question answers (ref. 66).
claims.note: Supported from Kutscher: median 55% (range 23-75%) of participants reporting any safer change in seven studies (eight locations) that did not introduce strips as a controlled intervention (refs 19, 38, 52, 55, 66, 71, 81; Supplemental Table 3 not read); reasons for using as usual (withdrawal, existing harm-reduction practice, tolerance or indifference, doubt about the result, wanting fentanyl); the review includes the Vancouver study (ref. 69) and the Rhode Island pilot (Table 3, Goldman 2019: 62 of 93 used at least one strip; Krieger 2018b is ref. 28). Not supported from Kutscher: 'mostly intentions' (see overstatement). Qualifiers: (1) the review names not using the drug (including selling or giving it away) among the most common changes, and Table 4 counts it in 14 studies, second only to smaller amounts (17). These are counts of studies, not of people, so they do not contradict 'seldom' as a share of people, but the reviews do not show discarding to be rare. (2) The top of the 23-75% range equals 702 of 937 instances (74.9%, editors' calculation) in the vending-machine survey relayed on AM p. 7 (ref. 81, one of the seven), so the median may mix instances and people; this cannot be checked without Supplemental Table 3. (3) Two before-and-after studies relay 68% (Rhode Island cohort of young adults who inject drugs, ref. 70, against 32% among those who did not use strips) and 67% (Baltimore, against 10% after a negative result) reporting safer change after a positive result. Ref. 70 is beyond the printed reference list (refs 51-95 are in Appendix 1, web only), so whether it is the claim's Rhode Island pilot cannot be told. If it is, a share with any change (68%) was reported, which bears on 'how many used the drugs as usual was not reported'; the editor should check this against Krieger 2018. (4) The seven studies behind the median do not include the Vancouver study (ref. 69); 'both reviews include' holds for the review as a whole, not for the median.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Seven studies that assessed safer behaviour change without introducing strips as a controlled intervention: median 55% (range 23-75%) of participants across eight locations reported any safer change (refs 19, 38, 52, 55, 66, 71, 81; Supplemental Table 3). Most common changes named: smaller amounts, not using the drug, going slower, a tester shot.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 5th paragraph (continues on AM p. 7)
anchors.extracted: People may use as usual despite a positive strip: to relieve withdrawal, because they already practise harm reduction, have fentanyl tolerance or do not mind it, doubt the result, or want fentanyl (refs 30, 80).

anchors.locator: Table 4
anchors.extracted: Studies documenting each change (actual / theoretical / total): smaller amounts 14/3/17; not using the drug, including selling or giving away, 9/5/14 (ref. 95 in both columns); going slower 8/2/10; tester shots 6/2/8; using with another person 5/2/7; naloxone at hand 5/2/7; using more or faster 2/1/3 (refs 66, 47; 94). The 'actual' column includes ref. 69 (Vancouver, staff-recorded intentions) and ref. 66.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Only two studies compared behaviour before and after strip counselling and distribution. Rhode Island prospective cohort of young adults who inject drugs: 68% with a positive result reported safer change, against 32% of those who did not use strips (ref. 70). Baltimore, 103 women who do sex work: 67% after a positive against 10% after a negative result; significant fall in self-reported illicit opioid and benzodiazepine use among those who used at least one strip (ref. 80). All self-reported.

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Vending-machine survey of 105 clients (ref. 81, one of the seven studies behind the median): strips from the machine showed fentanyl 937 times, with 702 instances of discarding the drug or using less (74.9%, editors' calculation; instances, not people).

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: People who use drugs often use harm-reduction tools and safer behaviours whether or not they use strips (refs 31, 37, 40, 53, 56, 62, 79), so change after a result is not attributable to the strip alone.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Goldman 2019 row; Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The review includes the Rhode Island pilot (62 of 93 young adults given strips returned 2-4 weeks later having used at least one) and the Vancouver supervised injection site study (ref. 69).

claims.overstatement: 'a darker line means stronger fentanyl' is more specific than the review, which reports only the mistaken belief that the line's intensity shows fentanyl purity and gives no direction. cl_dc_home_vs_service words it correctly ('the line's strength').
claims.note: Supported from Kutscher: the mistaken beliefs (line intensity shows purity; a negative strip means xylazine and a positive one rules it out); one participant saying a negative result would mean using a little more (ref. 47); riskier use (more or faster) in two studies (refs 47, 66); difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (refs 38, 39, 52); carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl reading negative and no information on other contaminants; no randomized trials, and only 2 of 91 studies with overdose outcomes, neither comparing people given strips with people not given them. Qualifiers: (1) Kutscher relays a figure on behaviour after a negative result: in Baltimore 10% of women with a negative strip reported a safer change, against 67% after a positive (ref. 80, AM p. 6). So 'no study read reports what people did after a negative result' (and the magnitude's 'No study reports behaviour after a negative result') should be limited to the primary studies read, or should mention this second-hand figure; it concerns safer, not riskier, change. (2) A possible harm the claim omits: a positive result may lead people whose drug of choice is not an opioid to believe wrongly that they have fentanyl tolerance (ref. 31, AM p. 7). (3) False positives and negatives, though rare, are said to confuse people and lower their trust in strips (ref. 58, AM p. 5). (4) Kutscher's 'six participants (1.8% of the sample)' (ref. 66) matches the take-home programme's 6 of 336, which are survey answers, not participants. (5) The review's authors conclude that handing out strips is warranted (AM pp. 8-9).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Misinformation reported: that the intensity of the test line shows the purity of fentanyl; that a negative strip means xylazine is present and a positive one rules xylazine out (refs 10, 30, 48). No direction (darker or fainter) is given.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 7th paragraph
anchors.extracted: A few participants in two studies used or would use strips to use more, or faster (refs 47, 66); one participant said a negative strip would mean using a little more because the drug would be weaker (ref. 47); another study: six participants (1.8% of the sample) reported riskier behaviour after a positive result (ref. 66).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips called easy but error-prone; positives five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme (ref. 66), read as possible contamination or poorer performance outside laboratories; difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (refs 38, 39, 52); false positives and negatives, though rare, confuse people and affect trust (ref. 58).

anchors.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph (begins on AM p. 3); Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl read negative (refs 15, 16, 25, 26); strips give no information on other analogues, xylazine, synthetic cannabinoids, phenacetin, levamisole or etizolam.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Baltimore, 103 women who do sex work given strips: 67% with a positive result and 10% with a negative result reported a safer behaviour change (ref. 80); self-reported.

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: People whose drug of choice is not an opioid: 80% reported theoretical safer change after a positive result (refs 30, 36, 57), but a positive result may also lead them to believe wrongly that they have fentanyl tolerance (ref. 31).

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No randomized controlled trials among 91 studies; only 2 of 91 report overdose outcomes.

claims.note: Kutscher has no data on the rural syringe-programme cohort (published later) and gives no median number of strips used. What it adds: few studies report a change in strip use over time (AM p. 6); 49% to 96% of participants across studies found strips useful and wanted to use them again (Supplemental Table 2, not read), so the 95-96% in the two programmes cited sit at the top of a wide range; participants in many studies felt that knowing only whether fentanyl was present was not enough where the opioid supply is mostly fentanyl, and the authors call single-drug strips increasingly outdated there (AM pp. 4, 8-9). This argument fits the suggested explanation for the fall in use but is not a measurement. Table 3 gives the Rhode Island pilot's return as 2-4 weeks after distribution.

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS distribution as a public health intervention, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Distribution studies mostly report numbers of strips handed out; few report a net change in strip use (in the number of participants using strips from baseline, or in how often they use them).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Overall satisfaction with use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 49% to 96% of participants across studies found strips useful and wanted to use them again (Supplemental Table 2).

anchors.locator: Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Many participants said that presence or absence of fentanyl was not enough to decide, especially where the opioid supply is almost all fentanyl; for people with tolerance the percentage of fentanyl mattered more; the authors call strips increasingly outdated among people who use drugs in many settings.

claims.note: The relayed statement is accurate. Kutscher cites four sources for it (Green 2020, Park 2022, Crepeault 2022, Wharton 2021), three of them not read here. The review gives no concentrations, brands or reading rule, so the editors' comparison with Bergh and Halifax for carfentanil cannot be checked from this source. Kutscher also says acetyl fentanyl and furanylfentanyl read positive, which fits the claim.

anchors.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph (begins on AM p. 3)
anchors.extracted: Only some analogues read positive (acetyl fentanyl, furanylfentanyl); others, including carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl, read negative (refs 15 Green 2020, 16 Park 2022, 25 Crepeault 2022, 26 Wharton 2021). No concentrations, brands or reading rule given.

claims.note: Kutscher relays about 96.3-98% sensitivity (and 89.2-89.4% specificity) for direct drug testing, citing Park 2022 (a validation study) and McCrae 2020, as the claim says. The review gives no concentrations, brands, reading rule or sample counts for these figures and did not appraise the accuracy studies (16 in this domain, Table 2). Its abstract and conclusion call strips highly sensitive and specific at the point of care, which goes beyond figures from drug-checking services and laboratories; the claim does not repeat that. The relayed limit of detection (0.100 mcg/mL, refs 7, 14, 15) fits the claim's 100-150 ng/mL. The claim could say that the relayed figures come without their conditions.

anchors.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips accurate for direct drug testing after dilution, limit of detection 0.100 mcg/mL (refs 7, 14, 15); about 96.3-98% sensitivity and 89.2-89.4% specificity for fentanyl (refs 16 Park 2022, a validation study; 17 McCrae 2020). No conditions or counts given.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions; Conclusion
anchors.extracted: Robust evidence for sensitivity and specificity; strips highly sensitive and specific when used at the point of care. Stated without appraisal of the accuracy studies.

claims.overstatement: The claim implies the review's list is wrong because the one source it names (Lockwood) found these drugs negative. Kutscher cites two sources for that sentence (refs 14 Lockwood 2021 and 16 Park 2022), and Park 2022 was not read, so the list cannot be called wrong on Lockwood alone.
claims.note: Supported: the review lists cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone (with methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine) as causing false positives at high concentrations, and says dilution prevents them (untested). Partly: the claim names Lockwood as the only source cited; the sentence cites Lockwood and Park 2022. Missed qualifier: the review relays specificity of 89.2-89.4% for direct drug testing (refs 16, 17; AM p. 3), that is about 11 in 100 fentanyl-free samples reading positive in those studies, without conditions; this bears on the claim's statement that how often false positives happen in real use was not measured. The review also relays that positives were five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme, which it reads as possible contamination or poorer performance outside laboratories (AM p. 5, ref. 66).

anchors.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph (begins on AM p. 3)
anchors.extracted: False positives at high concentrations of cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam, buprenorphine-naloxone, methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine, said to be preventable by dilution (refs 14 Lockwood 2021, 16 Park 2022).

anchors.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Specificity 89.2-89.4% for direct drug testing (refs 16, 17), without conditions or counts.

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Positives five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme (ref. 66); the authors suggest contamination or limits of strip performance outside laboratories.

claims.note: Both relayed items are accurate (difficulty interpreting 3% to almost 34%, refs 38, 39, 52; belief that line intensity shows purity, refs 10, 30, 48). On 'its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study': ref. 66 is beyond the printed reference list (refs 51-95 are in Appendix 1, web only), but ref. 66 is also cited for six participants (1.8% of the sample) with riskier behaviour, which matches the take-home programme's 6 of 336, so the identification is very likely. 'Five times' fits that study's crystal methamphetamine figures (27.6% against 5.2%, ratio 5.3) but not its cocaine (about 16 times) or opioid figures (equal), so the review oversimplifies it. Kutscher also says it is unclear whether training makes strips easier to use, with confusion reported despite training (refs 30, 53), which qualifies the take-home study's conclusion about accurate use with minimal training.

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips easy but error-prone; positives five times more frequent at home than at a drug-checking programme (ref. 66); difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (refs 38, 39, 52); false positives and negatives cause confusion (ref. 58).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Mistaken belief that the intensity of the test line shows fentanyl purity (refs 10, 30, 48).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Unclear whether training makes strips easier to use: some studies report confusion despite training, others better feasibility after it (refs 30, 53).

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 7th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ref. 66 is also cited for six participants (1.8% of the sample) reporting riskier behaviour after a positive result, matching the take-home programme's 6 of 336.

claims.note: Kutscher lists the belief that line strength shows purity as misinformation, says strips give no concentration and detect only fentanyl and some analogues, and lists contaminants they cannot show. These are the review's statements, second-hand; none is a tested finding, as the claim says.

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The belief that the intensity of the test line shows purity is listed as erroneous, with beliefs about xylazine (refs 10, 30, 48).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips detect only fentanyl and some analogues and give no concentration; in Canada mean fentanyl content 7-8.9% and over 16% of samples above 17.7% (refs 60, 82), all of which read positive alike.

anchors.locator: Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd continues on AM p. 5)
anchors.extracted: Knowing only presence or absence of fentanyl was not enough for many participants, and the percentage of fentanyl mattered more to people with tolerance; strips give no information on other analogues, xylazine, synthetic cannabinoids, phenacetin, levamisole or etizolam; many participants wanted fuller drug checking.

claims.note: Kutscher's figures match the claim: 2 of 91 studies; Vancouver, about 1% of visits with a check, post-use testing most common, OR 9.36 for intended reduction after a positive pre-use check, 0.41 for overdose and 0.38 for naloxone with intended reduction; vending machine, 10,155 strips in the first year, county deaths down 10% while Ohio's rose about 5%, confounded by naloxone and without a true control group. The review reads the Vancouver result causally (the prompt to reduce mattered more than the result); the claim rightly says it cannot show an effect. 'Neither with a comparison group' is the editors' reading: the review states the lack of a control group only for the vending machine, and the Vancouver comparisons are among checks, not between people who did and did not test. 'Crude' and '113 of the 120' come from the primary study, not from Kutscher. The machine gave out naloxone and other supplies as well as strips, as the claim says.

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only 2 of the 91 articles discuss overdose outcomes.

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Vancouver overdose prevention centre: only 1% of visits had a check and post-use testing was most common; among pre-use tests a positive result OR 9.36 for intended dose reduction; regardless of result, intended reduction OR 0.41 for overdose and 0.38 for naloxone use; the authors infer that the prompt to reduce mattered more than the result (ref. 69).

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Hamilton County, Ohio, vending machine: naloxone and other supplies plus 10,155 strips in its first year; 105 clients surveyed; Ohio overdose deaths up about 5%, county down 10%, overdose emergency visits down; confounded by naloxone, no true control group (ref. 81).

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only limited data suggest that strip use lowers overdose rates or deaths.

claims.note: Relayed figures accurate (documented use 1-80%, median 19%, Supplemental Table 1 not read; willingness 43-85% in five studies). The review includes the Rhode Island pilot (Table 3: 62 of 93 given strips returned 2-4 weeks later having used at least one; 66.7%, Wilson 56.6-75.4%, editors' calculation recomputed: same) and relays that only 1% of visits at the Vancouver site included a check. Table 3 shows the same spread in other programmes: Baltimore, 57 of 103 women returned and reported using at least one strip; syringe programmes in Baltimore and Delaware, 70% and 77% use; an emergency department, 18 of 23 accepted strips and 16 took them home. Kutscher's '2-4 weeks' differs from the claim's 'at least two weeks' (from Krieger), which the editor may check.

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Documented strip use 1% to 80% (median 19%; Supplemental Table 1), well below acceptability.

anchors.locator: Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Willingness to use strips reported in five studies, 43% to 85% of participants (refs 33-37).

anchors.locator: Table 3
anchors.extracted: Goldman 2019 (Rhode Island): 62 of 93 given strips returned 2-4 weeks later having used at least one; Park 2020: strips to 103 women, 57 returned and reported use; Park 2021: use 70% (Baltimore) and 77% (Delaware); Lima 2022: 23 offered, 18 accepted, 16 took strips home.

anchors.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Vancouver overdose prevention centre: only 1% of visits included drug checking.

claims.note: Kutscher relays one study (ref. 63, beyond the printed reference list; setting not given in the text) in which drug-checking services were used more often by people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected fentanyl exposure, injected in public, did sex work or had had a non-fatal overdose. This supports the direction (more often having seen an overdose). It adds own non-fatal overdose, which differs from the rural cohort in the claim (not clearly associated), and the claim's population (US and European studies) may not cover this study, whose country is not stated. Kutscher also notes that people who use drugs often practise harm reduction whether or not they use strips (AM p. 6).

anchors.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Drug-checking services more likely used by people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected fentanyl exposure, injected in public, did sex work, or had had a non-fatal overdose (ref. 63).

anchors.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: People who use drugs often use harm-reduction tools and safer behaviours whether or not they use strips.

key_findings.correction: Sensitivity, specificity, dilution and detection limit: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph (AM p. 3). The drugs in which strips detected fentanyl (heroin, counterfeit pills, xylazine-containing samples, alprazolam, cocaine, counterfeit Adderall, crystal methamphetamine, psychedelics): 2nd paragraph (begins AM p. 3, continues on AM p. 4). Checked on the rendered pages.

False positives and the analogue results: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 2nd paragraph (begins AM p. 3; these sentences on AM p. 4), not the 1st. The other two locators (Limitations..., 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph) are right.

key_findings.note: The review attributes the remark on confounding by naloxone and the lack of a control group to the primary study's authors ('As noted by the authors') and relays it.

reporting_issues.note: Recounted: years 83, designs 84, drug types 85; interviews 34 + surveys 12 = 46 against 39.
Six references for 'seven studies' (38, 47, 58, 66, 68, 69); three for 'two studies' (28, 38, 70); Table 4 has three for using more or faster.
Recounted from the rendered Table 4: ref. 95 in both columns for going slower, using with another person and not using the drug; distinct references 9, 6 and 13; the other rows have no overlap.
Ref. 20 is a medRxiv preprint, ref. 42 a Research Square preprint, ref. 29 a conference abstract.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall critically low agreed (critical items 4, 9 and 13 not met). Two domain notes, neither changing the overall: item 2 'partial yes' is generous, because AMSTAR 2's partial yes needs a protocol that plans a risk-of-bias assessment, which this review did not do, so 'no' is arguable; item 7 could be 'no' rather than 'no information', because the text describes each supplement (Appendix 1, full reference list; Supplemental Tables 1-3, use, satisfaction and behaviour change) and none is a list of excluded studies.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial rather than minor. The card's own 'claimed' text shows the problem. The abstract's headline (robust evidence of sensitivity and specificity, and of acceptability and feasibility of use) and the conclusion (highly sensitive and specific at the point of care) rest on two relayed, unappraised studies with specificity near 89%, while the body itself reports error-prone home use (positives five times more frequent at home, difficulty interpreting up to almost 34%) and low use (median 19%). The Results also infer a likely net increase in safer behaviour from uncontrolled self-reports. These are the review's most quotable statements. The overdose conclusion matches the results, which keeps the gap short of severe.

missed: Units in the behaviour-change median: the top of the 23-75% range equals the vending-machine survey's 702 of 937 instances (74.9%, editors' calculation; AM p. 7, ref. 81, one of the seven studies), while the review calls the median a share of participants, so the median may mix instances and people (Supplemental Table 3 not read).

Table 4's column of actual behaviour change after a result includes ref. 69 (Vancouver, intentions recorded by staff, as the review's own p. 7 says) and ref. 66 (very probably Klaire 2022, whose answers were to standard questions and may be hypothetical), so 'actual' overstates what was observed (AM p. 19).

If ref. 66 is Klaire 2022 (very likely), the review misreports it: the 'six participants (1.8% of the sample)' were 6 of 336 survey answers from 218 people, and 'five times more frequently at home' holds for crystal methamphetamine only (27.6% against 5.2%); opioid positivity was equal (90.0% against 89.1%) and cocaine about 16-fold (17.2% against 1.1%) (AM pp. 5, 7; Klaire 2022, Table 2).

The false-positive sentence (AM p. 4) cites Lockwood 2021 and Park 2022. If Lockwood found cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone negative, as cl_dc_fts_false_positives states (Lockwood not read by this reader), the list misreports at least one of its two sources. That dilution prevents these false positives is asserted, not tested.

The polysubstance field cites 'Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph' for detection in heroin, pills and non-opioid drugs and for false positives; those sentences are in the 2nd paragraph (as for key findings 4 and 5).
